newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke fights to restore government unity.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke fights to restore government unity.

text.p: Britain's Conservative government fought to restore an image of unity on Monday after a cabinet minister ruled out early entry into a European single currency and then backtracked a few hours later.

The flip-flop by Health Minister Stephen Dorrell reopened the ruling party's bitter internal strife over Europe, handing a propaganda coup to the opposition Labour party which is already tipped to win the election the government must hold by May.

It also highlighted the isolation of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, the most openly pro-European cabinet minister, who has fought a rearguard action to stop Prime Minister John Major ruling out single currency entry altogether.
Clarke, who said Dorrell called him on Sunday to warn him of the new controversy, went on radio on Monday to deny claims of a cabinet split over Europe as "froth and nonsense".
"Stephen declared yesterday... that he had not intended to change the policy...," said finance minister Clarke.

"We will make our minds up whether or not we are going to join a single currency at the sensible time when we see whether it's going ahead at all, who's in it and what the basic conditions are," he told a radio interviewer.
Major has tried to patch over the divisions in his party, which is now staring at defeat after 18 years in power, by adopting a wait-and-see approach to the single currency.
But Labour leader Tony Blair has shadowed his policy moves, increasing pressure on Major to take a tougher line against Europe to open up a policy gap with the buoyant opposition.
Cabinet ministers like Dorrell, formerly seen as pro-Europeans, have also shifted closer to the "Eurosceptics" who oppose moves to European integration.
Commentators say these are calculated attempts to position themselves for a post-election party leadership battle.

But after the size of the government's defeat in a by-election last week, which left it in a parliamentary minority and which if repeated in May would give Labour a majority of around 200 seats, the last thing Major needs is a new row over Europe.
The latest row began when Dorrell told a television interviewer "we shan't be joining a single currency on January 1, 1999," in apparent contradiction to the wait-and-see policy."
A few hours later he issued a statement through the Conservative Party Head Office saying: "I entirely agree with the government position and no words I used...were intended to question it," he said.
"We have not ruled out joining the single currency on January 1, 1999. We have said we believe the likelihood of our doing so is extremely small," he added.
Clarke's comments came just 10 days after he intervened in another row after Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said the government was basically "hostile" to a single currency.
Then, Clarke and Rifkind were forced to issue a joint late-night statement to paper over the divisions.

Labour said the latest confusion over Europe proved that the Conservatives were in complete disarray. "You can't understand what this government means from day-to-day and hour-to-hour," said Labour's deputy leader John Prescott.
